title: Amazon Interview Experience
author: TANU
body:
The Amazon interview process started with the Online Assessment. After clearing it, I was shortlisted for Round 1 and had only two days to prepare. I mainly focused on Amazon's 16 Leadership Principles, my resume, projects, and behavioral questions using the STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) approach. I also prepared guesstimate questions, supply chain basics, KPI tracking, and root cause analysis, but none of these were asked in my interview.My biggest advice is to quantify your STAR answers. Clearly explain the Situation, define your Task, describe the Actions you took, and finish with a measurable Result. Mention the size of your team, your specific responsibility, and the impact you created. For projects, clearly explain your role and include numbers wherever possible.

Some of the questions I was asked were:

Tell me about yourself.

Why Amazon?

Why Operations?

You are a Mechanical Engineering student, so why do you want to move into Operations?

Most of your internships and projects are in Design Engineering. How will those experiences help you in an Operations role?

Explain your projects and your specific contribution.

Multiple behavioral and situational questions based on Amazon's Leadership Principles.

What is your biggest achievement in the Cricket Club?

If your goal was to build a career at Amazon in Operations, why did you choose Mechanical Engineering instead of pursuing an MBA?

My Aircraft Landing System project was discussed in both interviews. While explaining it, I asked the interviewers if I could draw a simple sketch of the project. Drawing the project made it much easier for them to understand the design and my explanation, and it also created a positive impression. So, if you have a technical project, don't hesitate to use a simple diagram or flowchart while explaining it.After Round 1, I was shortlisted for Round 2 and had only one day to prepare. Since I had experiences from different clubs and leadership roles, I had enough situations to answer the behavioral questions confidently.Most importantly, be confident during the interview. Even if you don't know the perfect answer, stay calm, think for a few seconds, and answer confidently. The interviewer is not only evaluating your knowledge but also your communication, problem-solving approach, and confidence.Lastly, practice mock interviews (ChatGPT helped me a lot), ask 2–3 thoughtful questions at the end of the interview, and don't hesitate to ask for feedback.After successfully clearing both interview rounds, I was finally placed at Amazon.

All the best to everyone preparing for Amazon interviews! Stay confident, prepare your STAR stories well, understand Amazon's Leadership Principles, and practice explaining your projects clearly. Believe in yourself, keep improving, and give your best. I hope you achieve your dream of getting placed at Amazon. Good luck!

title: HCLTech Full Stack Web Developer Interview Experience
author: ARSHJOT SINGH
body:
Round 1: AI Bot Interview

The first round was an AI-based interview. It was relatively easy and focused mainly on my resume, technical background, projects, and questions related to the job role. Be familiar with everything mentioned on their resume and be able to explain their projects, technical skills, and contributions confidently.

Round 2: Hackathon

The second round involved a hackathon-style task where we were given a problem statement and asked to build a solution around it. For the Full Stack Web Developer role, our problem statement was to develop a ShopSmart AI application — an e-commerce platform similar to Amazon, enhanced with AI-powered features.

This round focused on understanding the problem statement, planning the solution, working with the team, and applying full-stack development concepts. Choosing your teammates wisely is extremely important, as effective communication, collaboration, and dividing tasks properly can make a significant difference.

Preparation Tips:

Revise CS fundamentals, especially DBMS, OOPs, Operating Systems, and Computer Networks.

Focus on JavaScript and React, including hooks, components, state management, and basic application architecture.

Choose your hackathon teammates carefully and focus on teamwork, communication, and task distribution.

title: Amazon 6M Winter Intern Interview Experience
author: VARUN ARORA
body:
My journey towards securing an internship at Amazon started with the Amazon HackOn 2026. After participating in the HackOn process, I received an Online Assessment (OA) opportunity, which was the first step towards the recruitment process. The assessment has 1 medium DSA question and one repository based debugging question.

After around a month, I received an interview call for round 1.

R1:

The first interview began with a brief discussion about my best project, where I was asked about its architecture and the technical decisions I had made, followed by 3 medium-level DSA problems, where I had to explain my approach, dry run it, write the solution, and discuss its time and space complexity.

The 1st question was based on Sliding Window, the 2nd question was a variation of the first, and the 3rd question was based on 2D Dynamic Programming.

After about a week, I recieved the call for round 2.

R2:

The second round started with the discussion about my resume and projects. The interviewer asked about the design choices I had made, the reasoning behind using particular technologies, and scaling related questions. It also included questions related to AI fluency, including how I had used Generative AI in my projects and how I would approach using AI to solve real-world problems. This was followed by 2 DSA problems, one medium-level and the other medium-hard, which required - to explain my thought process and optimize my solutions.

The 1st question was based on Monotonic Stack, and the 2nd question was based on BST.

And then around 3 days after the second round of interview, I got my result and here I am with the 6M SDE Internship at Amazon.

title: My Amazon SDE Internship Interview Experience: Article
author: KUSHAGRA
body:
When my name appeared in Amazon’s interview shortlist, I honestly didn’t know what to expect.

Like many students, I had been applying continuously to different companies, giving OAs, interviewing at startups, and facing rejections along the way.

So when I got shortlisted for Amazon, I was obviously excited, but I also tried not to keep my expectations too high.

A lot of things in the previous semesters had already taught me that no matter how much preparation you do, the final result is never guaranteed.

Still, this was an opportunity I wanted to give my best shot.

The First Interview (HM Round)

The first round was the Hiring Manager (HM) round.

Going into the interview, I expected most of the discussion to revolve around my projects, previous internship experience, freelancing work, and technical background.

To be honest, I was not expecting DSA right from the beginning.

But that is exactly what happened.

The interviewer started with a DSA problem that I would classify somewhere between Medium and Hard level.

For a moment, I was surprised because I had mentally prepared for project discussions first.

Thankfully, all the DSA preparation I had done over the past months helped me stay calm.

I discussed my approach, explained my thought process, and eventually solved the problem.

After that, the conversation shifted towards my projects and previous experiences.

There were questions about the decisions I had made while building projects, challenges I faced, and why I chose certain approaches over others.

The discussion felt more like a technical conversation rather than a strict question-answer session.

The entire round lasted around 1 hour and 15 minutes.

When the interview ended, I genuinely had no idea how it went.

I thought I had done reasonably well, but after enough interviews, I had learned not to make assumptions.

The Second Interview (SDE Round)

A few days later, I received the schedule for the second round.

This time, I was more mentally prepared for DSA.

The interviewer again focused heavily on problem-solving.

I was asked two DSA questions, both of which I would again place somewhere in the Medium-Hard category.

The challenge wasn’t just solving them.

The challenge was explaining the thought process clearly, discussing edge cases, handling follow-up questions, and writing clean code while being observed.

Fortunately, I was able to solve both problems and explain my reasoning properly.

The discussion also included questions around optimization and alternative approaches.

This round lasted approximately 1 hour and 25 minutes.

By the end of it, I felt satisfied because I had given my best effort.

At that point, the result was completely out of my hands.

The Waiting Period

For me, waiting after interviews is usually the hardest part.

Once an interview ends, there is nothing more you can do.

No additional preparation.

No additional coding.

No additional explanations.

You simply wait.

And after experiencing enough rejections in previous semesters, I had become comfortable with uncertainty.

I wasn’t assuming I would get selected.

I wasn’t assuming I would get rejected.

I was simply waiting for whatever came next.

The Email

The interesting part is that I didn’t first hear the result through the placement list.

Instead, I received a surprise email.

I remember looking at it and realizing that I had been selected for the 6-month Software Development Engineer Internship at Amazon.

Final Thoughts

If there is one thing I would tell anyone preparing for interviews, it is this:

->>>>>>> Focus on what you can control.

Build projects.

Learn continuously.

Practice DSA.

Improve communication.

Apply consistently.

The outcome is never guaranteed.

But preparation is never wasted.

Good luck to everyone preparing for interviews.

For daily updates, feel free to connect with me on X:

https://x.com/KushagraAg0717

title: Amazon SDE internship placement experience
author: HEEMANSHU KUMAR GUPTA
body:
By: heemanshu gupta

Title:Amazon SDE Internship Placement Experience (6-Month Internship)

Content: I recently secured a 6-month Software Development Engineer (SDE) internship at Amazon through the campus placement process.

The selection process consisted of an Online Assessment followed by interview rounds. The Online Assessment focused on Data Structures & Algorithms, problem-solving, coding, and logical thinking. Consistent practice on coding platforms and a strong understanding of DSA fundamentals helped me perform well in this stage.

The interview rounds included coding questions, discussions on projects mentioned in my resume, computer science fundamentals, and behavioral questions. Interviewers were interested in understanding my problem-solving approach rather than just the final answer. Whenever I got stuck, I explained my thought process, asked clarifying questions, and worked through the problem systematically.

Some key factors that helped me during preparation were:

Regular DSA practice and mock interviews.

Strong understanding of projects mentioned in my resume.

Preparing examples that demonstrate teamwork, leadership, and problem-solving skills.

My advice to juniors is to focus on building strong fundamentals rather than memorizing solutions. Start preparation early, stay consistent, and participate in coding contests and mock interviews. Confidence, communication, and structured thinking play a major role during interviews.

I am grateful to the placement cell, faculty members, seniors, friends, and family for their support throughout the journey. I hope this experience helps future aspirants prepare effectively.

Result: Selected for Amazon SDE Internship (6 Months). 🚀

title: Amazon (Operations) Interview Experience
author: HARINDER SINGH
body:
Workstyle Assessment
Amazon places strong emphasis on Leadership Principles. This round involved scenario based questions where I had to choose responses aligned with principles such as Ownership, Customer Obsession, Bias for Action, and Invent & Simplify. Reading the Leadership principles beforehand helped a lot.

Technical and Behavioral Round
The interview started with basic introduction questions followed by problem-solving. I was asked to explain my recent projects, especially the parts involving data, automation, and decision-making. This round evaluated how I approach real workplace situations. All questions followed the STAR format (Situation, Task, Action, Result). Some examples included:
• A time I handled a difficult problem independently
• A situation where I disagreed with a teammate and how I resolved it
• An example where I reduced errors, improved a process, or optimized a system
Preparing 6-7 solid examples in advance really helps here.

Key Tips:
Go through Amazon’s Leadership Principles thoroughly.
Build clear, structured STAR stories for behavioral questions.
Understand your resume well, projects are often the deciding factor.
